description: To design and build an interactive game or app that lets kids ages 7–12 manage a lunar or Martian outpost, making real decisions about life support, radiation shielding, power budgeting, food production, and communication delay, and experiencing how those choices play out over the course of a simulated mission.
summary:
AstroCommand: Deep Space Survival is a browser-playable 3D space outpost simulator developed using React, Three.js, and Vite for children aged 7–12. The game allows players to take on the role of a lunar or Martian commander, explore an interactive planetary base on foot or by rover, and monitor nine life-support and habitat systems through a holographic dashboard.

The project addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge through an interactive, consequence-driven emergency decision system. When events such as dust storms, radiation alerts, or oxygen failures occur, players must choose between two possible solutions, each with different benefits and consequences. This helps them understand real engineering trade-offs involving power, life support, radiation shielding, and resource management.

AstroCommand makes space science engaging by combining realistic mission challenges with immersive 3D gameplay. It encourages children to develop critical thinking, problem-solving, and systems-thinking skills while learning about the challenges of sustaining human life beyond Earth. Inspired by NASA’s Artemis and Mars exploration missions, the project transforms complex space engineering concepts into an accessible and enjoyable learning experience.
details:
AstroCommand: Deep Space Survival

1. What does it do or how does it work?

AstroCommand: Deep Space Survival is an interactive 3D space outpost simulator designed for children aged 7–12. It allows players to become space mission commanders and manage an outpost on the Moon or Mars. Players can choose their role, destination, and difficulty level before starting their mission with a 3D rocket launch.

Once they arrive, players can explore the outpost on foot or using a rover, collect scientific samples, repair equipment, and operate different habitat systems. A holographic dashboard displays nine important resources, including power, oxygen, water, food, crew health, and radiation shielding.

The main feature is its emergency decision-making system. When situations such as dust storms, radiation events, or oxygen system failures occur, the game pauses and presents two possible solutions. Each option has its own benefits, costs, and consequences. Players must think carefully because their choices can affect both current resources and future mission conditions.

The game also simulates communication delays between Earth and the outpost, helping players understand why astronauts on Mars must often solve problems independently.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Makes space science more interactive and enjoyable for children.
  • Helps players understand how life-support systems, power, food production, and radiation protection work.
  • Develops critical thinking and decision-making skills.
  • Teaches resource management by showing the consequences of different choices.
  • Encourages exploration through 3D environments and rover activities.
  • Provides a browser-based experience without requiring downloads, accounts, or a dedicated server.
  • Supports replayability through different missions, roles, difficulty levels, and randomized emergencies.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main goal of AstroCommand is to make children curious about space exploration and help them understand the challenges astronauts face beyond Earth.

The project aims to develop systems thinking, logical reasoning, resource management, and problem-solving skills. Instead of simply learning space facts, children experience how one decision can affect multiple systems in an outpost.

It also aims to inspire young learners to explore STEM fields such as aerospace engineering, planetary science, and robotics. By making mission challenges interactive and recoverable, the game encourages children to learn from mistakes and try different strategies.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

Programming Languages

  • TypeScript
  • HTML5
  • CSS3
  • JavaScript
  • GLSL shaders

Frameworks and Libraries

  • React 19 – Building the user interface.
  • Three.js – Creating 3D graphics and environments.
  • React Three Fiber – Integrating Three.js with React.
  • Drei – Providing reusable 3D components.
  • Tailwind CSS – Styling the interface.
  • Zustand – Managing game state and simulation logic.

Software and Tools

  • Node.js and npm
  • Vite – Development server and build tool.
  • vite-plugin-singlefile – Creating a portable single-file web build.
  • Web Audio API – Generating game sound effects.
  • HTML Canvas – Generating procedural textures.
  • localStorage – Saving mission progress.

Hardware

A standard laptop, desktop computer, or touchscreen mobile device with a modern browser and WebGL 2 support. Keyboard, mouse, or touchscreen controls can be used.

5. How is your project creative?

AstroCommand combines space exploration, 3D simulation, and interactive decision-making into one educational game. Unlike traditional space learning applications that mainly provide information, this project allows children to actively explore and manage a space outpost.

Its creativity comes from several features:

  • A fully interactive 3D lunar and Martian environment.
  • A futuristic holographic mission control dashboard.
  • A two-option emergency system where every decision has meaningful consequences.
  • Animated astronauts, rover exploration, rocket launches, and equipment repairs.
  • Randomized emergencies that make each mission different.
  • Simulated communication delays that demonstrate the challenges of deep-space missions.
  • Procedurally generated terrain, textures, visual effects, and sound effects.

The most creative element is that the game does not simply label choices as right or wrong. Both solutions can be useful depending on the player's resources and mission situation.

6. What factors did your team consider?

During development, the team considered the following factors:

  • Age-Appropriate Design: The game uses simple language, clear indicators, and only two options for each emergency to make it understandable for children aged 7–12.
  • Scientific Accuracy: The game is inspired by NASA's Artemis, Mars exploration, space-weather, and life-support research. Simulated values are clearly distinguished from real-world data.
  • Gameplay Balance: Emergency choices are designed to have meaningful costs and benefits without making the game unfair.
  • Performance: 3D graphics and particle effects are optimized to support smooth gameplay on standard devices.
  • Accessibility: Color-coded alerts are supported by icons and text, and touch controls are available for mobile devices.
  • Replayability: Different planets, roles, difficulty levels, and randomized events keep the game engaging.
  • Learning Through Mistakes: Mission failure leads to a safe evacuation and debrief, encouraging children to learn and try again.
  • Easy Access: The game runs in a browser without requiring accounts, downloads, or paid assets.
